name: Ivan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I've done a few of these surveys for the union, but never one that promised I could be honest, so let's see how that goes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Westmoor, which is about 1,100 acres of wheat, oilseed rape and grass, with 900 ewes. The land's owned by a pension fund in the city, which is a joke I'll come back to. My day starts at six with the weather and a call to the shepherd, Dougie, then it's sprayer plans, grain stores, buyers, and walking the crops, because no screen tells you what a field smells like. I've got four staff and two seasonal lads, and I'm the one who stands between them and the land agent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the joke about the pension fund?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That I manage land for a pension fund and I haven't got much of a pension myself. Pay's poor for a manager on an estate this size, and Meena, my wife, is a healthcare assistant at the district hospital, so we're not rolling in it. We've a few weeks of savings at best. The kids, Arjun and Leela, are grown and doing fine, thank God, but we've nothing put by for a rainy decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest, but kindly. At the union branch I'd say it's a good thing, because it buys us time to sort out pay and pensions without a robot hanging over every conversation. Online I'd probably share some article about it and get two likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've still got to fix my own money problem, and nothing's going to fix it for me. Hype or not, I'm 58 with a thin pension. AI fizzling out doesn't put money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, but use the time. I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone for the odd job, like drafting the stewardship grant forms, which honestly saves me a whole Sunday. And I'd start paying a bit more into the pension, even if it means one less takeaway a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because it's the same old squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it saves you a whole Sunday on grant forms. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I had a hedgerow grant application, forty pages of the stuff. I typed my notes into the AI on my phone and it laid it out in plain sections, and I checked every line. Meena found me in the garden at two o'clock instead of at the kitchen table at ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Westmoor would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dougie, the shepherd. He's 63 and he's had two hip operations. AI or no AI, his body's going to give out before his pension starts, and the fund won't care.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good thing because it buys time to fix pay and pensions without a robot hanging over every talk. I'd say it at the union branch and probably share an article online.
S0.think: I think I've still got my own money problem, 58 with a thin pension, and nothing's going to fix it for me. AI fizzling out doesn't put money in the bank.
S0.do: Carries on as manager and keeps using AI on his phone now and then for grant paperwork. Pays a bit more into his pension each month, cutting a weekly takeaway to cover it.
S0.feel: Calm, with a flat sense of the same old money squeeze.
S0.quote: Meena found me in the garden at two o'clock instead of at the kitchen table at ten.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI already, in a measured way, and his example was specific and believable. His real concern is retirement money, not technology. He immediately turned the conversation to an older colleague's health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a proper transition plan. If tasks are being taken over, workers should share in the savings, not just the fund's shareholders. I'd say that at the branch meeting and probably in the local paper's letters page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a pension fund would be quick to do it. They already ask me every year where I can cut labour, and robot weeders and drone spraying would give them an answer. My job's probably safe for a while because someone has to run the machines, but Dougie's and the lads' aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the neighbours' trials first, I'm not going to be the one who buys the expensive mistake. Once a couple of farms had the robot weeders working, I'd go on the course and learn to run them. And I'd get the union to negotiate a deal at Westmoor: no one goes without retraining and a year's notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, yes. I can see a way through for me, but not for everyone I manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the neighbours. How long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One full season, maybe two. I watched the Hendersons buy a fancy auto-steer in 2019 that never worked on our slopes. I'd rather be second and right than first and broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a gap between what you'd say at the union and what you'd do as the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I lie awake on it. As manager I'd be the one bringing the machines in and drawing up the staff plan. I'd try to do it fairly, but I'd still be the one doing it.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a transition plan, with workers sharing in the savings and not just the fund's shareholders. I'd say it at the branch and in the local paper.
S1.think: I think the pension fund would move quickly, since they already ask every year where to cut labour. My own job is probably safe for a while, but the shepherd's and the young workers' aren't.
S1.do: Waits one or two seasons to see neighbours' robot weeder trials, then goes on a course to learn to run them. Gets the union to negotiate a deal at Westmoor guaranteeing retraining and a year's notice for staff.
S1.feel: Uneasy, seeing a way through for himself but not for everyone he manages.
S1.quote: I'd rather be second and right than first and broke.
S1.fieldNote: He holds two roles at once, union member and the manager who'd bring the machines in, and he named that tension himself. His caution is grounded in a neighbour's failed purchase. He is protective of his staff more than worried for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has failed, plain and simple, and that we need emergency support for workers now, not a report in three years. I'd be at the union rally and I'd probably make a speech, which Meena would hate. I'd say the robot companies should be taxed to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, if it comes in 2028, I'm out. Why would a pension fund pay a manager when the AI plans the crops and the robots do the work? I'd be sixty with a few weeks of savings and maybe one other estate manager's job within fifty miles, and that'll be gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within the first month I'd sit down with Meena and go through every outgoing. We'd cut the second car, the phone contracts, everything. I'd sign every workers' petition going and push for a fund levy on robot owners. And I'd ask Arjun, quietly, whether we could lean on him for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. I'd be lying in bed doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between this and having more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time to build anything. I can't save a pension in two years on my wage. With more time I could at least work out a plan with the fund, but with two years they'd just send me an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Arjun quietly. Why quietly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm his dad, and I'm supposed to be the one who helps. He's got a baby coming. It would be the hardest phone call I ever made.

S2.say: I'd say the government has failed and workers need emergency support now, paid for by taxing the robot companies. I'd be at the union rally and would probably make a speech.
S2.think: I think I'd be out, because a pension fund won't pay a manager when AI plans the crops and robots do the work. I'd be sixty with a few weeks of savings and almost no other jobs nearby.
S2.do: Goes through every outgoing with his wife in the first month and cuts the second car and phone contracts. Signs petitions and pushes for a levy on robot owners, and quietly asks his son about leaning on him if needed.
S2.feel: Properly frightened, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: With two years they'd just send me an email.
S2.fieldNote: He switches from manager to worker here, seeing his own role as easily cut by a remote owner. His public anger is about policy, but his private fear is about money and pride. The phone call to his son was the moment he went quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd say there's no excuse: the government and the big landowners have time to plan, so let's see a plan. I'd get the union to run training days for farm workers. I'd say proper support is a choice, not a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. That's still short of a pension, but it's long enough to learn the new kit and make myself the person who runs it. I'd probably keep a job of some kind, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get on the robot and drone courses at the college, once a couple of neighbours had shown the kit works. I'd put every bit of overtime into the pension. And I'd make sure Dougie gets an early retirement package out of the fund, because I'd fight for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the sort of worry you can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make yourself the person who runs it. Is that what you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Want is a strong word. I'd rather walk the fields than watch screens. But I'd rather run the screen than be run over by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Meena think, if you tell her this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's heard me make plans before. Then she'd say, alright, but you're not missing Leela's wedding for some robot course. Which is fair.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough warning that the government and big landowners have no excuse not to plan. I'd push the union to run training days for farm workers.
S3.think: I think five years takes me to 63, short of a pension but long enough to learn the new kit and become the person who runs it. I'd probably keep a smaller job of some kind.
S3.do: Goes on robot and drone courses at the college once neighbours have shown the kit works, and puts all overtime into his pension. Fights for an early retirement package for the shepherd from the fund.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan, a worry he can work with.
S3.quote: I'd rather run the screen than be run over by it.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years turn him from frightened to planning, which fits his wait-then-adopt habit. He still wants proof from neighbours first. The fight for the shepherd's retirement package is consistent across every scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it that's on the politicians. I'd say every farm worker should get paid training and a decent pension, funded by the people who own the robots. Same speech, with more time to give it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I'd be done anyway. The worry for me is the gap, whether I can save enough over ten years to retire at 65 with Meena and not be a burden. The work itself I'd stop worrying about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Westmoor and bring the new machines in slowly, once proven, with the staff trained up first. I'd plan to step down at 65 and hand over to whoever's learned the kit. And I'd vote and campaign for a pension top-up for low-paid workers, that's the policy I'd care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but more about money than about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would you be doing in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do nothing new with the land, honestly. I'd sit with Meena and a pension adviser and make a real plan for the first time in my life. Then I'd get the shepherd's and lads' futures sorted with the fund before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you'd keep working past 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my knees let me and if it's teaching. I'd like to show young people how to read a field, robots or not. But I'd not hang on in a job a machine does better, that's just pride.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be on the politicians. Every farm worker should get paid training and a decent pension funded by the people who own the robots.
S4.think: I think at 68 I'd be done anyway, so my worry is saving enough over ten years to retire at 65 with Meena. The work itself I'd stop worrying about.
S4.do: Keeps managing Westmoor and brings new machines in slowly once proven, with staff trained first. Plans to step down at 65, sees a pension adviser in year one, and campaigns for a pension top-up for low-paid workers.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more about money than about robots.
S4.quote: I'd not hang on in a job a machine does better, that's just pride.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his concern shifts entirely to retirement savings. He wants to hand over well rather than hold on. His views on public support and worker ownership stay consistent throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the machines, for the speed. What would help is a proper transition fund for farm workers, paid for by the people making money from the robots, and a pension top-up for people like me who spent thirty years managing other people's wealth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Whoever owns the robots will own the farming, and that's already the pension fund, not the people who live here. I'd like to see farm co-ops own the machines, the way this valley once owned its own creamery.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the robots will own the farming, and that's already the pension fund, not the people who live here.
portrait: Ivan Patel is 58 and manages a large wheat, rape and sheep estate owned by a city pension fund, on a wage that leaves him with only a few weeks of savings. He's a union member who also has to bring in the very machines his union worries about, and he says so openly. He uses AI on his phone now and then and adopts new kit once neighbours have proved it. He is calm in the plateau, frightened by AGI in two years, and with more warning he turns to planning his retirement and protecting his staff, especially the ageing shepherd.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because of the speed; with two years the fund would simply email him and he'd have no time to build a pension.
whatWouldHelp: A transition fund for farm workers paid for by those profiting from robots, and a pension top-up for low-paid workers like him.
